projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Orlando Ribelli was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran, Orlando Ribelli, also known as Larry. Larry served in the U.S. Army Air Corps with the First Fighter Group, Headquarter Squadron. He served in the European Theater, mostly in Italy. At his highest rank was Tech Sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Ribelli's home in Mentor, Ohio, on May 12, 2001. Larry was 79 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: I've lived here for 23 years, since '77. I lived in Cleveland the rest of my time. So, I was in and out of hospitals in the Cleveland area. I was in the Veterans Hospital there at times. But mainly, I retired from Euclid Incorporated, making off -- off-highway trucks. And before that, I worked at the body shop for GM on Euclid Avenue. And that's about my civilian experience.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Your hometown during the war was?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Smithmill, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: I was born there. In fact, we just sold the property recently. And my wife is from the same town. We were pretty well service-minded. She had six brothers who were in the service, out of eight boys in the family. They were a family of 12. There were only three in my family, my brother and sister. I lost my brother. But I was fortunate to spend the time that I spent in the Air Force.

I went in on a dare. I went in at the age of 19. I -- I graduated high school in 1940. I -- I paid -- excuse me -- I played some semi-pro baseball in South Jersey for my first summer. I was in a car accident around August of '40 and the injury put a stop to my baseball career at the time. I went back to PA, was hunting with a good friend of mine, and he was a little older than I, and he knew that he was going to be called up for the service.

So, he wanted to go in early and pick his own service. So, he dared me. I didn't even think of service life at the time. He says, "You're a chicken." And on that dare, I went in, thinking that I probably wouldn't pass the physical because of dental work that I needed. But they -- they took me and we went to Harrisburg. We're sworn in. We had a choice of either going to Langley Field, Virginia, or going to the Philippines.

Well, he wanted to go to the Philippines because of the two years overseas was considered a three-year course, when you get out two years early. And I says, "No way. I want to stay in the states." So, we flipped the coin and I was a winner.

Every time I look back on that now, the importance of that and why I'm pointing it out, he and I would have been in the March Bataan, because we were going to go to Bakers field, and that was taken over by the Japs early. And I always considered myself lucky by the flip of the coin. And -- and from then on, I've -- we went on maneuvers there, the summer of '40. I was in the hurricane in New Orleans and Mississippi area. And then, from there, we come north.

Believe it or not, I really enjoyed the first part of my life as a serviceman. But mostly, after the war, I think it was two days after December 7th, we were on a train going north, assuming that we're going to, probably, New York to get on a boat. Fortunately, we didn't. We were stationed. We were put up in a big apartment building in New York and we worked at 90 Church Street, in conjunction with the Navy. We were antisub. We were First Bomber Command at Langley. We become the antisub command because we were chasing subs, in conjunction with the Navy. We were flying the Atlantic Ocean. We had something like 15 squadron from Mifflin to Cuba and Key West, Florida. And what we were doing, actually running pattern flights in, and we had designated areas to fly.

I did -- I did go up. I wasn't an aerial man at all, but I used to volunteer and go and we'd be out there six, seven, eight hours at a time. We sighted subs at times. We'd call the Navy in and they would drop their depth charges. We didn't know whether there were any kills or not, because they kept that to themselves. But that was about all I did in the states, other than I become unassigned and not needed as the war progressed. We cleared the Atlantic Ocean enough that it was pretty free traveling on it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This would be in 1942?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: And they start disassembling the antisub command and I was -- I become unassigned, had the six stripes, and I decided to go to cadets, flying cadets. So, I was accepted and went to Goldsboro, South Carolina. I think it's South Carolina. I get them confused, north and south. It's been so long. But I had passed all the exams and it was seven days of written and physical combined and they -- we were accepted, most of us, we were going in rank, and they were going to send us to Pittsburgh, Pitt -- Pitt University, for pre-pre ____.

They were going to give us a fast course, two-month course, and we go to pre-pre flight. Well, the night we got the news that we were going, the following morning, they made us fall out and told us we weren't going. They says a new system was being looked at, they had taken a good analysis of the whole situation, as far as the war was concerned, and they considered the situation, that they had enough cadets to -- to finish the war out.

They knew just about when the war would end, the way we were going, and they had enough college boys coming out of college to fill any openings they might have needed and since we had all the rank and we had been trained, we were going to be sent to have others sent back that have been overseas, maybe, some of them, up to three years, especially the one I -- I replaced, the Master Sergeant in the First Fighter Group. That's how I got that --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why don't you give the breakdown of the unit that you were in. The First Fighter Group --

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: The First Fighter Group, Headquarter Squadron. I was in the Headquarter Squadron, where we used to lay out the daily missions. That was our function, mainly. And then, the separate squadron pilots for that day, that mission, would all get together and we'd have the maps set up and the rendezvous point of coverage for the bombers. We were -- I was in the P-38 Fighter Squad or Group. The 15th Air -- 15th Air Force. It was considered heavy bomber and fighter. We were combined.

The whole 15th Air Force had both, both heavy bombers and fighters. I think I would have stayed and made a -- a life deal out of it. The only thing, I'd seen too many young guys that I had met come back from missions no sleep, from Ploesti, on those missions, running out of gas and crashing. There were times -- there was one time in particular we sent 48 airplanes out to give coverage of the bombers on a mission to Ploesti. Only six returned out of the 48. 42 of them were scattered all through Northern Italy and Ploesti and the Hungarian area and the Slovenian area, Yugoslavia. A lot of them had to ditch in the water, in the Adriatic.

In my function, other than just sitting up at the map, I had the job of corresponding with missing in action families from the states. The minister that was assigned our group and myself handled all that. Come in and we'd interrogate other pilots that might have seen someone get shot down or whatever happened, certain flights. It was up to us to correspond with the families and some of those letters are really heartbreaking.

I served there in Italy. I met ____. My folks were Italians and I visited their areas. My dad was born north of Italy, north of Rome, and I was able to go up there. I was there a day after the Germans were run out of the town. In fact, the machinery was still on fire and smoking in the fields when I arrived there and I was lucky to get a flight up in the area, one of the small planes. Before that -- I kind of jumped myself -- in the Southern France invasion, I went over to Corsica and we spent a month over there. Not -- not the whole group, but we split the group. I went over with -- with that group and then the others stayed in our group near Foggia.

The 15th Air Force was situated in Bari, which was south. And by the way, the -- I was on the convoy that went over. We were only the second convoy that ever stopped, pulled into Bari. Everyone who went before us that ever pulled up that far north, because the Germans are not too far up, and we -- we moved according to how fast the infantry had moved, of course, the ground forces moved the Germans back.

And actually, we tried to get up close to cut down the mouths that we had to fly, so we wouldn't run a few. The Germans, the pilots used to come up and scare our pilots into dropping their -- their utility tanks. They all carry tanks with extra gas in them, they go on these long missions. What they would do is just come up and fake it that they were going to attack. And then we'd drop our tanks, utility tanks, and we'd be caught short on gas. That's why we had so many planes that had to force down on the way back from Ploesti. I left Italy two months after the war. We tried -- we had to clear up the -- the planes and material, but I come back. Now, there's an incident that occurred before I even went overseas that I jumped kind of out of place.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's okay.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: 19 -- the latter part of '43, when we were breaking up the antisubmarine command, I -- I took a furlough and I went back to my hometown, knowing that it was so unpredictable what was going to happen. So, while I was there, a friend of mine, a neighbor really, we grew up together, was back and he was in one of the ground forces, Captain Butner (ph), and he was kind of depressed and I asked him what was wrong.

He says, "Well, I'm in this dog gone ground group." He says, "I want to get in the Air Force like you're in, in the Air Corps." And I told him, I says, "Well, listen. I can tell you how to do it, how you can get in very easy. But I want you to promise me one thing." And he says, "What's that?" And I told him, "You want -- you want to go there," I said, "and if they wash you out, like they washed me out," I says, "I want -- I don't want you taking any secondary flying things, such as radial gunnery, tail gunner, things like that." I says, "I want you to let me know and I'll tell you how you can get in my outfit, wherever I might be." And he says, "Okay."

So, I went on to tell him how to do it and he went back and he did the same thing and he immediately was picked up, being high school graduate at least, you know. And sure enough, after about three weeks, he found out he was washed out, unacceptable, but they gave him the secondary choice of radial gunnery and he didn't get to me. He left it go. He took it. He wanted to fly that badly.

And we -- we lost him three months after he had gone overseas on a certain mission. Before that, when I had told him all this, in his conversation, we went to visit the town that we graduated high school from, which was seven miles away. In fact, my high school days, I walked and hitchhiked seven -- seven miles each way. And I played all sports, varsity sports. Anyway, I had good friends down there and I found out that two classmates of mine were home on furlough, and so, he and I, Buddy and I, his name was Buddy Woodurk (ph), his dad and my dad both came from the same town in Italy. In fact, I saw his great grandmother when he was missing in action, this Buddy Woodurk (ph).

I spoke to his grandmother and I had to relate to her that he was missing in action, they didn't know, because there were no corresponding. Anyway, we went down to visit and the four of us were sitting at my friend Graham, Frank Graham's home. It was Tom Maturna (ph), Frank Graham, and myself, we were in the same class, and Steve Woodurk (ph), Buddy, we called him Buddy, he was a year behind us. We all sat together kidding and joking, never thinking that, gosh, this is the last time I'm going to see any of them. And that's what happened. And all three of them get killed in Europe, none in the Pacific.

The two, the Tom Maturna (ph) and Frank Graham, both got killed in the Fifth Army in Italy. So, that was another reason for my not going back in. We -- I came from a town that only had about 300 people, and out of that, I think all eligible men about my age had gone in the service. We lost seven out of the group that went in the service and that's a pretty big percentage for that many men who -- men in the service.

In fact, our whole area in Pennsylvania that I came from, there were an awful lot of casualties. If not casualties, they were serious fatalities, as far as injuries, legs, arms being lost. In fact, one of my best friends back there is still living there and he was -- he lost a leg at Salerno, in Italy, in the Invasion of Salerno.

But the highlight of my service was the fact that I was able to witness so many things happening. Our outfit was always handed the most prestigious things that occurred overseas, inasmuch as giving air protection when President Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin met at the Black Sea. Well, we gave President Roosevelt coverage from the African coast all the way into the Black Sea. Our outfit was chosen to do that. And there were other incidents that occurred that we were given first choice.

I sat -- I was an Air Operation Specialist, that's what they called me, sitting at my desk one day and I get this radio teletype or message, "P-80 left (Maniples) At such and such an hour," and that was only about 20 minutes or so earlier than I got the message. And we heard the jet going overheard, ready to land. In fact, he was calling in for landing instructions with our tower and we had it at our base for training purposes. We were the only one in the European Theater to have a jet from the states. We didn't have jets. The Germans did.

That's why they sent this one over because we were losing our talon charlies on our missions. That was the last plane in the flights and no one up front could see what happened. What they were doing with the jets is coming in quickly, making one swipe and "boom." They're either killing them or, you know, whatever, destroying them or making them land, making them crash land. So, finally, they found out what it was by accident. Some stray pilot of ours happened to look out the side and seen this happening and that's why they brought the P-80 over.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: P-80. Shooting Star is what they called it. And I'll never forget that because we had it roped off and we had our pilots, all -- most of them that wanted to check out in it, got to take it up. In fact, the colored outfit that was stationed next to us, the 52nd Fighter Group, in fact, the -- the Colonel was in charge of that become an officer in Mayor Stokes' regime in Cleveland. I can't remember his name anymore, but he cleared out in it. In fact, he used to come in the office there and we used to talk a lot.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that Davis we're talking about?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Davis. Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Benjamin Davis?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Benjamin Davis. Because when he was in office, I called him one time, just wondering if I could get through, and I got through. And I explained to him who I was and when I told him Operations, First Fighter Group, he remembered right away. I says, "Shooting Star," and he says, "Oh, yes." He says, "You gave me my clearance." He says, "I used to clear flights." And other than that, do you have any questions?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: We need to get your rank.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: I was a Tech Sergeant when I -- when I got out of the service. When I was discharged, I was a Tech Sergeant, five striper. I lost one stripe overseas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did you lose a stripe?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Commanding Colonel and I didn't agree on a lot of things. I was a regular Army, by the way. I wasn't called up or anything. And during the Southern France Battle of the Bulge, they were taking Air Force men and putting them in the infantry and all that. And I had pretty good information, I had friends in the states that worked in publications, where I had worked for some time, and they kept me up on anything that might be of interest to me, in protection.

And my good friend, that's passed now, been gone 15 years, he wrote me a letter one day, and he says, "Hey, for your benefit, put this down," he says, "in your book." He says, "The circular so and so, number so and so, date of so and so," he says, "they cannot transfer you, since you're regular Army, to a lower echelon outfit." In other words, anything other than the Air Corps, they couldn't transfer me unless I wanted to go, I made application to go. So, he says, "Just keep that in mind." He says, "It might be an advantage for you." Sure enough, the Bulge come up and I had no training really, you know. He says -- and actually, he and I didn't get along because there were other things that happened along the way that I used to call him on and question him. And he checked it out.

His Chief Clerk called the 15th Air Force, because we didn't have all the circulars there, and they checked it out, and it's word for word what I had said. So, the only way that -- he was a reservist. I says, "Colonel, you can go before me." I says, "But I know what I'm talking about. I'm regular Army. You're not moving me unless I want to be moved." I says, "Even -- even in an emergency like this," I said, "I'm not shirking my duty," I said, "I'm just being tough on you because you've been tough with me." There was a lot of things that come up, they wanted to break me when I first went over there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why is that?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Because I was coming in with a lot of rank and they were trying to give the rank -- see, they have the tables of organization. They're only allowed so many Masters, so many Techs, so many staffs, and all that. And my coming in, I was replacing a guy rank-in-rank, but they wanted to promote the guy that had been over there all that time. I -- I couldn't blame them in a way, but they were forgetting about me and my service. I had over four years service and they were going to break me because that's not my fault that I got over there late. So, he backed off. He sent -- I didn't want them to send any of the guys because we weren't trained for that, you know. They were sending them to slaughter really. But there were other incidents that occurred. When I went to -- back to the -- on point systems, that's why I pointed out those different five -- those are five point bonuses, all them in there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Those campaigns there?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Yeah. All those campaigns gave us an extra five points towards our being sent back. Well, I had the points. I didn't say anything at the beginning. I left it go for a month or so. And finally, I told them, I went in, I says, "You know, I've got the points legitimately to be sent back." He says, "Yeah. But you haven't been over here long enough." He says, "We got guys with more time over here than you."

I said, "I'm sorry. Most of those guys don't have as much time as I have total." He said, "Well, you should have come over earlier." I said, "Listen." I says, "I was supposed to go to the Eighth Air Force." The Eighth Bomber Command was being formed. We had Colonel -- Colonel Williams that come to the outfit and he was in the southern parts of our nation, and down in Panama and that area, and he lost a lot of flying time and I did him a favor when I was in -- working in the office in New York, at Mitchell Field in New York. I picked up a lot of flying time for him that he had lost and I -- we got him the command pilots thing, which is -- in name, which is a big thing for them, you know, for Generals, and he was so taken aback by it that I was able to pick up that time for him by -- I did it on my own, with the help of the Operations Officer.

All he did was sign the papers for me, the forms. That he was destined to be the head of the Eighth Bomber Command when they were forming it. He was going to be Commanding General of it, Big General. He asked me, he came down the hanger line one day, and he says, "Hey, Sergeant, this and this is going happen." He says, "Well, we -- we heard rumors, but nothing for sure." He said, "I'm going to become the B.G. of the Eighth Bomber Command." He says, "How about you coming with me?" I said, "Gladly." I wanted to go overseas because all that time in the service, you know, you only get out.

He said, "Okay. I'll talk to your Commanding Officer," who is Headquarter Squadron. And he went up to talk to him. He said, "No way." He says, "I can't let him go." He said I had 50 students that I was teaching my job. I was teaching them so they could scatter them all through the U.S.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Tell us a little bit more about what your job was.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Well, I kept all flying time of the pilots. In the states, we had operation orders. Any flight that was made, we'd record that in writing; name, serial number, and all, that had -- that were going on these trips back and forth. We'd mark down the arrival and departure times. We had a file, technical file for all our airplanes. Complete files on the airplanes we had. I used to apply for the flying time money, extra money they got, the percentage that they got per month, and made sure that they got their four hours or more a month flying time in. And other than that, we generally -- I used to have a little gambling thing going on. Yeah.

We used to have a big, long map table. That's right. The pilots would come in and want to go to St. Louis or places like that, Florida, wherever. They'd ask me to get them a set of maps and I'd get the maps out and route it for them and put the times on it that they could arrive. They'd have fuel and all that. We were like second pilots really, not flying at all, but we -- we had this big map table in the operation office. That's what it was.

And we had four enlisted men then and the mechanics used to come up every now and then, especially when we weren't too busy, in bad weather. We'd flip half dollars to the end and see who got closest to the end. I used to keep beer money. But we used to, like I said, we used to write up the orders and compiled what we called the "Form five." That's -- that's how the time was recorded. And then, we'd get senior pilot ratings for them and command pilot ratings for them as they come up. But that was generally -- then, in between, when they'd change engines on an airplane or overhaul an engine, we'd go down there on our spare time, put our coveralls on and work with them, you know, play volleyball in the hangers, especially bad weather. But Mitchell Field in New York was a great place because you always had an outlet to go to New York City.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: In New York City, we lived at the Benjamin Franklin Apartments, 77th and Broadway. We used to travel by subway to 90 Church Street, down near Canal Street, and down there where the money was at. The -- the big banks and all that. That's --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wall Street.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Wall Street was right there. In fact, the oddity of the whole thing is I've got a nephew that's working in the same building where I was in the service where he's in the banking deal. They just moved in there. So, but -- but as -- generally, military life was great for me. If I hadn't seen so many young men lose their lives, burn up and, you know, crash land, I -- I would have stayed and made a life out of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't think we specifically found out why you lost your stripe. He just one day took it away?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: No. I bad mouthed the Colonel, bad mouthed the Colonel.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He busted you?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: And I wouldn't apologize because I thought I was right. He couldn't break me completely down to private. I says, "Give me a three-day pass." And he says, "What do you want a three-day pass for?" I says, "I'm going to go to the 15th Air Force Inspecting General and explain my case." It's the only way I had as your appeal way. Well, when I said that, he didn't like it because the words that were said, and the people that overheard our argument, we used to argue profanely. I mean, oh, yeah. We'd cuss each other and everything. But his name was Colonel Roberts, from Texas. Proud Texan. But he was -- he was a reservist. And he was always mad at me because I used to remind him of that. He was nothing but a reservist, you know, and he almost killed us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How's that?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: When we went to Southern France, it's the first time I ever saw him fly a plane. We had a B-17 that was out of service, it was only, we -- we -- we used it like a transport. Well, we loaded up our typewriters and our maps and all that and we went to take off. And he wasn't that good of a pilot. He didn't know enough to know that you had to really throttle that thing to go. You had to full throttle it on takeoff.

Well, we got up there about 75 feet and we were jumping like that. And one of the second lieutenants went up and grabbed him on the shoulder and pulled him right out of the seat. Well, he knew I knew that because I was up there right behind him. I was in the -- in fact, I was in the radio seat, radio man seat. And he knew I knew that and I used to -- I brought that up.

I told him one day, I says, "Hey, you're a flunky. You're not even a good pilot." Oh, coming back, after I did -- the way I got to come back, he didn't want to send me back. He was going to keep me over there. He had -- he had -- he couldn't do it. He -- I went in to see him, I says, "No. I got the points. I want to go back to the states legitimately." And he says, "Nope. I'm going to keep you here to clear up all the planes."

He says, "They're -- they need men in the 15th Air Force to clear everything up." Well, they threw most of them in the water, planes and everything. You'd be surprised. At any rate, that argument went on for about a week and I was ready to -- very mad on the deal. You know, I knew that I had to come back because physically, I had a lot of _____+ cyst bothering me. They wouldn't operate on me over there. It was continually draining on me.

So, I told him the second time or third time, he said nope. So, I went on sick call and they sent me to the 21st Station Hospital in Foggia, Italy, and my doctor kind of sympathized with me because he had the whole story and he was a Pennsylvanian too. So, we were, you know, buddy-buddies and we made him a lot of money on -- on our softball team. He used to bet on us and we were the champs of the 15th Air Force and all that. Anyway, he went to bat for me. He sympathized with me. He said, "No. You should go back." He said, "I've talked to the Colonel." He said, "But he's" -- he said, "You two have something going for each other, so, you're both stubborn." He said, "Now, I want you to do this. You go to the Station Hospital. You see Captain so and so," and he called him. He told him I was coming in. And the captain said, "Oh, no. You're Dr. Esposito's (ph) boy."

And I said, "Why?" And I said, "I've got a problem." I said, "But, you know, I want to go back to the states legitimately. I don't want to force the Colonel to send me back, not that way." He says -- he examined me and he said, "Yeah. You should have that taken care of." He said, "In fact, it should have been taken care of earlier." I said, "Yeah. But they wouldn't do it." They -- they cleared it up, dried it up with Penicillin, 45 shots of Penicillin. I was in the hospital for two weeks. Everyday they were giving me two shots, two or three shots a day. But I got, you know, 40 some shots.

And he says, "Well," he gave me an envelope and he says, "You take this back. You hand it to your Colonel." And I didn't ask any questions. So, I went back and I went in, and actually, I knew the Chief Clerk. He was a Sergeant Major. They didn't call them First Sergeants. In Headquarter Squadron, you didn't have no First Sergeant. And I handed it to him. And he starts smiling. And he says, "What is this?" And I said, "Just give it to the Colonel." And he went in and knocked on the door. We used -- we used an old barn as an office, but we used lime on -- on the walls and that, like paint. We were pretty clean. He knocked on the wooden door to go in and he went in and he gave it to the Colonel and I'm sitting in the -- in the room there. I didn't leave because I wanted to hear his explanation. His -- I wanted to hear what he said when he first opened up the envelope. And he says, "That son of a bitch." Here, what the Captain had told him is you either send back by points, and he's got enough, or I'll send you back on the ship, medical ship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: So, he knew the medical ship would have been a very good way to go back, you know, you wouldn't be among another 8,000 guys. So, he come out there and I was still there. He says, "Oh, you're still there." I said, "Yeah. I just wanted to hear screaming in there." I said, "I knew you were going to scream." I said, "I didn't know what was in that letter," I said, "but the doctor did tell you you should send me back legitimately." And I said, "And if you were the man I think you possibly could be, you would send me back that way." So, he -- he says, "You're excused. Get out of here."

So, I left and he sent word up to me that I was going with the next group and they had it posted and actually -- well, the day that we were leaving, he come out and he -- the deal he did with all the groups that were leaving, so many were leaving every week or so.

Anyway, he come out and shook hands with all the guys. He wouldn't shake hands with me. Because I -- you know, I had beaten him almost at every turn. We were on a eight-by-eight truck pulling out, a big truck. I'm on the endgate end of it, and I'm like, "Hey, Colonel." He run over to his Jeep and he had second thoughts. He had second thoughts. He decided he better not. Let it go. But he said goodbye to everyone but me.

Can -- can you imagine? But mainly, some of it was my fault too. I used to aggravate him. I used to ask him when he was going to go on a mission. He wouldn't go any missions. And that used to bother me because there were some that he could have gone on, you know. But they wanted to save their cans. They didn't want to get shot down. They didn't want to get hurt. You'd be surprised how many pilots we had that were scared to fly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: One in particular, I felt sorry for him. He was legit. He didn't -- he didn't fake it. You know, some of them faked it to get out of it. But some would start a mission out and come up with something wrong with their thing and come back before they even got really started. And one in particular wouldn't even fly. He quit. He said, "They can do whatever they want with me." And I felt very sorry for him. I could imagine a guy getting depressed that way, being scared, because I'm getting somewhat depressed that way in my life now. See, because physically, I'm -- I'm very -- I looked all right, but I'm in pretty bad shape. My diabetes and all that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, you didn't tell me, he sent you back on points, I assume?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Well, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh yeah. That's what it --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He wouldn't put you on the medical ship?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Oh, no. Oh, no. He wouldn't give me the better of the two. But you know, I found out later that any one that he ran across in the service or after the service in Texas there, from the First Fighter Group, he would always asked about me. He -- in fact, he even told someone he even -- he liked my spirit. He says he liked the fact that I kept up with the WD Circulars and that coming through. Little did he know that I had good informants in the states, see.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, that's -- yeah. I guess I didn't ask you that. How were they able to get that -- get letters to you with information like that?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: You mean from the states?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: They'd mail them to me from the states. It was open. The letters weren't intercepted going from here to us over there. Ours were coming back. But heck, the -- the guy that used to check my letters, I worked for him. He's outside of Pittsburgh now. Swakard (ph) his name was. He come up through the ranks too. He was a private in Langley Field, Virginia, when I was in there. In fact, he was on the garbage detail and I used to kid with him.

And I went overseas and here he was, an officer, a pilot, with wings on him. Jeez. Yeah. He come back. I just called him up not long ago. I found out -- I joined a group, the Fighter Group that I was in, and they have a good strong organization. They meet every year or two. They just met in California this year. Now they're voting for the next one, which is going to be in 2002. And they gave us a chance to vote in three places, for three places.

Like, they were -- thought about Boston, California, and Las Vegas. And it was voted in Las Vegas. However, in the meantime, the group that's stationed at Langley Field, Virginia, now, that's their home base. Fortunately, that's where I took my training. And someone from down there, the younger First Fighter Group boys, want to maintain that same system over -- after we're all gone, because we're pretty well depleted. There's not too many of us left.

In fact, I lost a guy from Madison here just two months ago. He was a pilot in the 71st that I knew and I seen him off and on. And they -- they ask for a revote and they explained why. So, we choose Langley. If I'm still living, I'm going down there if I have to be carted down. Yeah. I'll get my brother-in-law or one of my sons to take me down. Because it's quite a thing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This -- this is the First Bomber Group where you're talking about?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: No. The First Fighter Group.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The First Fighter Group, rather. So, this -- there wasn't one of these in Franklin, Pennsylvania, was there?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That must have been the Squadron. The last -- actually, several of the places you're talking about, you know, he --

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Well, he would know -- he'd know this Swakard (ph). See, he come up through as an enlisted man, a flight pilot. He didn't come out as a Second Lieutenant. Because, evidently, he didn't have the background that most of the pilots at that time had. A lot of them are coming out of West Point. Most of them were college graduates. This guy happened to come up through the ranks, you know. And he was the best pilot the First Fighter Group had, World War II. In fact, I think he was the best.

He saved at least 75 pilots in airplanes over Ploesti the one time because of the wind. They were going there and there was a recall. So, if they go in the mission, the weather comes up bad or gets spotty and they can't see the target, they'd have a recall. They'd come back. Well, the recall was given at about 50 miles from target. And he decided -- in fact, he told the whole Squadron, he got the airwaves, which you usually don't do, and he told them, he says, "Well, we're this close, let's get a counted mission, let's get over target." And they went over target and just as they did, the skies had opened up and a bomb group that was stationed right next to us near Foggia, Italy, were over -- over the target dropping their bombs and these Jerrys were up there ready to attack them.

And we come in and shooshed them away. But they come back and they were telling us about this, you know, that they took a chance in going over target. Well, low and behold, an hour or so later, this bunch of trucks coming from the Navy field, from the bomb group, they come over with their liquor and everything to celebrate with these guys that saved their ass. They knew that they would have got all shot up, especially over Ploesti. You fight them and you got dinged up a little bit, you never make it back. We used -- we lost more planes and lives in the Air Force I think over Ploesti than any other place in the world. We -- it used to be a shame.

I used to pray all day when those guys were going on a mission. From the time they left until the planes landed, I prayed, hoping they'd make it back. Then, right away, if -- if only a few got back, you want to know where the others were at, if there's any hope for them. Most of them would get back, if they were still living. You know, a lot of them would get killed. But if they were still living and had to force landing at -- because the people in Yugoslavia and Northern Italy, they were on our side for that. Italy -- Italy had no heart in it after they -- after the United States got in the war. They didn't want anything of it.

After Africa especially, they wanted out of it. In fact, when I visited my uncle at Rome, right -- he lived right across from the Vatican, and I was visiting there for about a day. I had gotten there, I was going to spend a week with him. My cousin come out of the Army. He went A-W-O-L from the Italian Army. He was a First Sergeant. And when he saw me in the house, he didn't know who I was, you know. He thought maybe I was a military policeman or something like that there to pick him up. When he found out I was a cousin. And he was still living there too. I was in contact with him there not long ago.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the full name of that pilot that you were talking about before?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Jerry Swakard (ph).

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Swakard (ph).

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: He was in the 94th, but he was assigned to -- see, what they do, they assign officers from the Squadrons to the Headquarter Squadron. We -- we, as a Headquarter Squadron, only had enlisted men assigned. The officers were loaned. The Operations Officer was from the 71st from the time that I was over there. In fact, he makes all our paperwork, magazines, and he writes articles. This pilot from Madison says he's the biggest BSer in the Air Force, because he makes up stories, you know, they're not authenticate.

Well, he makes himself look good. But then, the one Major that was in -- in command of the 71st Squadron, I'll never forget him because he used to spend most of his time in the group hall with us. They'd come down there and BS, the commanding officer from each squadron. And he used to come in there and he'd brag about being the youngest major and all that. And I pointed out to him one day, I says, "There are a lot more that are as young as you or younger, that's nothing to brag about." I says, "The thing that you should be able to brag about is being a good pilot and how many planes you shot down, the enemy." I says, "Then I'll listen to you. But as far as your age and being a Major, that doesn't even phase me. That doesn't even phase me."

And this Swakard (ph) that went up through the ranks and all, he'd just laugh. Because he would never turn one down, a mission. He'd -- if one of the guys had to drop out or something, had the flu or something, he'd take their place. And in fact, the Colonel, that's one thing I did like about Colonel Roberts, although I had all our arguments with, he did protect Swakard (ph) because Swakard (ph) would have killed himself, you know, if they left him go.

You have the extremes. We had the extremes. You had the ones that didn't want to fly and you had the ones that you couldn't stop flying. They'd keep going. He had something like -- like 65 missions before he even thought of coming home. That's a lot of missions. Some of them are pretty rough.
(End Track One.)
(Begin Track Two.)

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: We had 24-hour duty. There was no such thing as line personnel or anything. The whole field was operated. We had -- normally, they loaded bombs with the lift, hydraulic lift. We loaded them from the back. Four GIs would have a 500-pound bomb on their backs and bring it up to the plane and they had the guy hooking them up and pulling them up in the plane. As fast as the planes would come down and pull up, just like an assembly line, that's how fast we were loading them, because we knew the guys were getting it, they were getting it bad. There was -- the news coming back from the fields, they were getting causalities like -- like crazy and we had to do something. That's the only thing we had to do, especially the enlisted men, you know.

But we worked. We worked our buckets off for about one week. Finally, they had to taper off because some of us couldn't take it anymore. That's a lot of lifting, you know. You know, we weren't used to it. But that and up at the foot of the mountains going into Rome, where they were embedded in underground, and we were hitting the monastery. Well, we spent months up there trying to get them out of there. The Germans were in there so tight, and boy, they battled us. That -- that whole western coast of Italy, from Salerno on up, from Sicily on up, we had it rough, Air Force and infantry, especially the Fifth. Montgomery on the other coast was doing good. We'd get way up ahead and wonder where our boys were at. But he didn't have anything like we had on that coast, had the mountains and all that. Italy was -- I was kind of disappointed in my service in Italy.

See, I went overseas, April '44 is when I left the states, early '44. 28 days on the sea in a convoy. 110 ships on convoy. They knew the destiny. They told us we were going to Bari, Italy. We'd be the second group to ever go in there. And for some reason, Hitler's birthday was the 21st of April. I'll never forget that. 21st or 22nd. And we were just off north of the -- on the -- on the -- not the Adriatic. Mediterranean. We were just north of Algiers. On the eve of his birthday, eight -- they sent eight airplanes down. There was a mixture. Junker-88 and a couple other types. They shot two of our -- they got two of our depth-charge-two boats. One had nothing but women on it, wax, the other ones were all GIs. And I was the enlisted man in charge on our ship.

We had a Captain that was in charge and an enlisted man. The enlisted man actually gave -- put names up on rosters to help out, like, in KP and all that and, you know, cleaning, sweeping down the deck. I remember the next day, I was up on deck when they come over. It was like dusk in the evening. And we were smoking our last cigarette and sitting up there. The weather was real nice. And these planes come over and we thought -- we were looking for escort going through the Mediterranean, because, you know, hey, we weren't too far. Southern France was an hour, half hour away really. And we heard these engines, but we were rushing to go on the other side of the ship to watch the planes come in, and I yelled, I says, "Those are German airplanes," because the sound is -- the sound is different. Their airplane engines sounded different than ours. They were noisier.

And sure enough, they come in. I looked up and I saw depth charges coming out and they were firing their 50 calibers and whatever they had on them. They were shooting at us. And you could hear the bullets hitting the concrete tops. One guy got -- well, when they hit the ships next to us, they got an oiler -- an oil carrier and two liberty ships. The two liberty ships, one on each side of us, and the -- the oil tanker was behind us. They got all three about the same time. And I happened to look up and our gunnery, Navy gunners, got the one plane, shot him up and he went into the water. But we went down. They -- they yelled on the intercoms, "All -- all GI -- all soldiers, go to your quarters."

And I go -- go to your hole really. What a place. A hundred octane gas underneath. The whole hold, you take it up and underneath there's nothing but 56-gallon containers of hundred octane gas. Can you imagine? You can -- you can tell very well why those two ships went up right away because they hit the bottom. Boom. And the next day, the Captain come over to my bunk, he said, this is before daybreak, he says, "Sergeant," he says, "I want you to get ten of your best men, men that can keep their mouth shut and are real strong minded." He says, "We're going to go out and clean the top deck of the ship."

And it didn't strike me at first, you know, what he meant. But then, as I was starting to get the names together, the guys -- some of my best friends that I knew were on board, then I started thinking, it might be, it must be something real bad. We went up there, there are parts of arms and legs and clothes and duffel bags, whatever. Glasses, eyeglasses, and that. Well, when those ships went up, that debris went in the air and come down, hit the top deck of our boat. It was up -- I got sick. I had to puke. I had to go on the side and puke. It was hard for me to take. And all the ten guys I had with me were working in conjunction with the Navy boys, sweeping the whole deck down and water hosing it all down. But that's one of the worst spots.

In fact, that's where my _____ started, because when we get hit and the -- those concussions of the exploded boats around us and I -- it blew me off the deck and I come down on my rear end. It was always there, but that started it. You know, it started working.

But then, we went into -- from there, we made it to Bari. Didn't have no other incidents. We pulled into Bari, Italy, and I spent a week there and then they all figured out where we were supposed to go. In the meantime, they assigned me in charge of the unloading the guard duty on the ships. They had the natives unload and running the cranes and whatever and I had to move around. Each one of us had a ship to guard. And I get a few men running around, you know. These guys were working on it, the native Italians, you know, and they're talking among themselves.

You know, we got cigarettes over here. We got this and got that. And I called them all together, I says -- I told them, I says, "Any of you guys have" -- and I told them in Italian, the little I could talk, at that time it was very little, but I picked it up quickly because the first six years of my life my dad taught me Italian. That's all he spoke at home, he and my mother.

And people used to tell them, "What are you doing that for, Fred?" He says, "Listen, I got him now for six years." He said, "But after six years, he's going away." He says, "He's going to thank me some day for that." You know, that six years, that knowledge that I gained then, helped me out tremendously. But anyway, these guys were talking about how they were going to take cigarettes and that and this and that from -- from different packages. They -- they were going to loot.

I told them, I says -- you know, I showed them my gun. I says, "See what I got here?" I says, "It wouldn't take much for me to shoot you guys. I catch one of you guys sticking your hands in any of these packages and things," I says, "you guys will get your brains blown out." Boy, they just looked at me. They didn't figure I could understand Italian, see. But boy, they -- they did good work. They did good work because you paid them, we paid them well. And they -- throughout my service in Italy, I always got the interpreters job. Any interpreting to be done with the villagers, most of the airstrips and fields were built on farm land and each farm land had a big mansion, whatever it was in those days. They're pretty old because they're passed down through the generations.

She -- the lady that owned our land that we were on, the First Fighter Group, lived on the hill from us. So, I got pretty familiar with her because I used to have to go up with the check and everything. It was in a sealed envelope for payment for rental. We were paying rental.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Paying rent for --

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Oh, yeah. For the use of the land. Well, we were kind of tearing it up some too. Putting all the steel grating down and all that. We were using all the buildings. Up until the war happened, they had people giving so many acres that they could work and they would contribute so much of the product to the owner and then she thereby would sell it. That's how they made their living. But I got to know her pretty well. In fact, she even invited me up for some meals and -- but I enjoyed that part of it.

But I was ashamed of the people. Mostly they turned out to be -- of course, the war did that, become beggars and they'd steal from you if you weren't careful. But that comes from poverty and needing. But I was ashamed of them really. Even my relatives, I went on up to visit them, I had an aunt that lived between Foggia and Naples in a hilltop community and it actually spiraled up.

And I went to visit her. Her husband, she met him, he was in the service and he happened to be up around Rome and she was a young girl named Mary and he was a barber. And I went up to visit and the girl -- they had two girls. They were both a little younger than myself. And I was only 20, 21, 22 at the time. And their friends were all communists. See, from Foggia down, in that area, even then, they were communists. You had to be careful. Your -- like I told the people, their friends, "I'm a soldier. I'm not in government. I have no politics. So, I don't even want to hear it."

But some of the guys were kind of radical, you know, and they wanted to know why I didn't think the way they did, you know. And I told them, I said, "I don't talk politics. I'm a soldier." And the girls just -- I used to tell the girls this, my two cousins, and they -- they'd even broke up with some of those kids. They weren't friends with them anymore. Because when I come back a few months later, before I left for the states, they told me. I told them too, I says, "Be careful how you choose friends in -- and then politics." I said, "They get you in a lot of trouble." And they kind of looked at it kind of tightly and they broke away from it.

But there's parts of Italy that was really radical communists. There was a lot of people in my hometown, one time when -- when I was a child growing up, of course, it was in the '20s, there was a poverty stricken area, really, you didn't have two nickles or a rope together. It was mostly Italian, Irish, some Scotch men, and a lot of Ukraines. My wife is Ukrainian. But when I went over -- overseas, I was kind of -- I had forgotten the background, my background is living.

Well, when I visited my dad's hometown and then the town next to it, where most of the Italian people migrated to my hometown in Pennsylvania, these kids were all growing up and born pretty near the same time I was because they all come over, migrated to Pennsylvania or to the United States about the same time. So, all these kids growing up were pretty much my age. And I remember all the kids pretty well, face-by-faces and names. And I walked through this one neighboring town where my dad was born. There were more from that town that they called Canale. It was in -- in Viterbo area, that was like providence [sic], the Viterbo providence [sic], which would be like our counties.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Okay.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Okay. And then, my dad's hometown was ____ Romano, which is also in that same providence [sic]. In fact, that's where I landed in Viterbo and by air. In -- in the -- in my dad's neighboring town, I walked in, there's one main street, and they were -- all these people worked in the farms, like I -- I had explained before. Most of them were home at the time I was up there because it was on holiday. They come home for festa, what they called festa, celebrations. Well, I was walking through town, I'd tell the kids on the street who they were. It -- if not the right name, it was a relative, like an aunt or an uncle that lived in Pennsylvania. Well, they ran home. These kids off the street run home and was telling their parents, "I don't know where he come from, but he -- he knows us, he knows so and so, our aunts and uncles." Well, then the old people come out, when I explained to them who I was, they knew right away. We had a -- they had a guy in that town played a -- an organ, a hand organ. What do they call that?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Accordion.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Accordion. By gone, that day we were there, it was a Sunday -- Sunday afternoon, he was playing his instrument in the home that he was living in and I was listening and listening and I says to the -- some of these people that I was talking to, I says, "Is that so and so?" "Yeah. How do you know? How do you know?" I says, "Well, he lived just a couple houses from where I lived." I said, "I used to watch him play." But there's so many coincidences that happened, occurred to me while I was in the service. It's unbelievable sometimes.

But, oh, my uncle that lived next to the Vatican was -- was an electrician. He had fallen off a scaffold and had ruined one of his shoulders, so he had to retire. He couldn't work anymore as an electrician. But he took me through Saint Pete's, the whole Vatican, and he explained it to me step-by-step and the history of it. I can't even remember half of it. He explained it to me. Now -- but at that time, he did -- did a wonderful job. In fact, I was up there Christmas of '4 -- '44. Yeah, Christmas of '44. One of the most miserable days of my life standing in the Square, Saint Peter's, waiting to get in. I was on my feet in a size one under my regular sized shoes.

I had boots that I bought on the flight to Africa and I wore them for dress. And one of my most miserable days of my life. I stood in line to get in, a couple hours, and then the church had stand about an hour and a half, the seats were all taken. I got home that night, I had to cut them off. I mean, to my -- where we were staying. I had to cut the boots off my feet. But I saw Pope Pius XII make mass that night and I thought that was -- that was great, but you had to do it suffering. And Rome, Italy was nice. And Naples, awful. Worst than Baltimore. Baltimore is a pretty dirty town, down near the ____ in downtown. Naples is just as bad, if not worse. And those people --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything you remember in particular about entertainment or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Oh, overseas we had a lot of entertainment. We had Bob Hope and all that. All those troops would come in. In the states, in the states, of New York City, we had the run of the city. We could go to any stage show, any -- any place at all down around Time Square. They had three major league baseball teams. We were able to go to any of them. We were treated best out of the three ball fields at the Giants, treated us the best. They were the poorest of the three in the city. Brooklyn wasn't bad. But the Yankees were terrible as far as treating soldiers.

I mean, they let you in free, but they put you in a place where they wanted you and you stayed there. But Brooklyn and the Giants, you could move around, if there were empty seats. All they asked you is if anybody carrying a ticket claimed a seat, you had to move. And most of them come in, had tickets, and you'd be sitting there, they just take a seat behind. You know, they didn't always have the place filled up, other than when the Yankees played St. Louis for the World Series, then it was filled up. But I was lucky, I got tickets.

I lost my can there too. I lost over two thousand dollars betting on that. The Yankees won their first game, I won about five hundred dollars. And then, they lost four straight after that. I was taken for about four or five hundred bucks a clip. Throughout my service, I was real lucky gambling. I always had oodles of money. Never -- never was I under a thousand in my pocket in New York City. When we went on maneuvers, I had the whole outfit broke. I broke them all playing Blackjack.

We went to New Orleans, I was the only one, including officers, that had any money, because we hadn't gotten paid for about two months. And I formed a line. I was banker for that weekend. I had to give each one of them money. So, I -- I got sick of that, so I broke it off quickly. And I -- I said, "Hey, I'm going to go with you guys in town. I'll pay your way." You know, the big red light district there. I shouldn't say that. But I bought them all a fifth of liquor and got them in this big stretch limousines and had them taken to their -- you know, they had them all over the city. Took care of all of them. I was the talk of the Air Force for about six months. They wanted to borrow money and half the time they meant well, but they'd be transferred to something, you'd never see the money, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: And I would never believe them if they give them more than so much. Because forget it. It's just like giving it away. But half the time I took the money from them. So, that was one way of giving it back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything in particular about the Bob Hope Show overseas?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Oh, no. He was always great. Bob -- Bob Hope was always great. He would put on an hour and a half show like nothing. There were so many shows, you know, and I'm sorry. I've forgotten so many of them too. There's a lot of things in my career, when I was in the service, that I forgot, especially some names and that. I may be in the bed some time and I'll come up and I remember it, certain names. But you'd be surprised how quickly you forget.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: But we used to get these guys come over. Bob Hope, I saw him at Foggia. Some of them we saw in Bari, the short time I was down there. But most of those guys, they come over in singles or maybe two or three and put on a show, especially a comedian or a singer, and they'd have their music, four or five-piece band. They -- they kept us busy. We were lucky at Foggia, being in the 15th Air Force, we had a big place in town. They took -- they took over a big ballroom in there and that was our USO and had beer and all that. Had a good price. I had a good long furlough in Venice, went A-W-O-L for a week. Yeah. They used to fly us up there on leave, rest camp. They called it rest camp. I was up there two weeks.

During the two weeks, I met a girl from Slovenia and she was there, a big -- nice blonde girl. And I'm not -- I'll never forget that. That's the first time I got Blue Ribbon beer and they had it up there for the GIs and you were allowed something like a case, 24 cans, for the stay. And I had mine and had carrying it around the campus bag with ice in it and I went out on the beach, Lido, and I fell asleep. Drank about four or five beers and got to me and I fell asleep.

I woke up, somebody was rubbing my back. Here she is putting oil on my back because I was burning up. She tried to wake me, couldn't wake me. She finally got me awake, but that's what she was doing. And I spent the rest of the week, I used to take her to meals with us. We had -- we were staying at the nice hotels. This was after the war, though. This wasn't -- the war was already over, in that two-week -- two-month spread before I come back. So -- but I went A-W-O-L for a week.

I missed the plane. We were supposed to be at the airport to come back a certain date and they made sure when they dropped you off, "Don't forget, you have to be back here such and such an hour, such and such a date." Well, I didn't go. I stayed an extra week. But I had problems there. The dialect -- the Italian dialect was one I couldn't understand. Vietnamese [sic] -- the Venice people spoke a different dialect all together. But that was a lot of -- like the states there, you go south, you can't understand some of those southerns.

But in Italy, it was even worse. Primarily, the reason for that was we weren't that well versed. You see, all the Italian folks come over around 1910 to 1915, they made their own language. In other words, they -- they'd speak in Italian, but they'd give it the English version too. So, the words were not authentic Italian. You know what I mean? And it wasn't English either. The next place nearest to that was on the Island of Corsica. You had Italians and French that had that island over the years, over and over, and they spoke half Italian, half French. But that -- that island was so much like Ohio and Pennsylvania for the streams that run through it, the countryside, about the same. Beautiful.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What else did I want to ask you here. Oh, you said you got back, in what, August of --

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: 28th. I was discharged August 28th.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any trouble adapting to civilian life?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: No. I loafed the first year because of my back. I was on more -- more or less cabincy, over -- recuperating from the operation. And then, I had to go back to -- to get cleaned up again. Oh, by the way, the only reason why I'm in this area is because of that problem, the ____ cyst. I went well over a year before it completely healed up. And I was worried that maybe it was more than just that. I thought maybe it was cancer. And I had some friends that worked here during the war, come back, and they talked to me and asked me if I was doing anything and I told them no. And they said, "Why don't you come out to Ohio." And I told them my problem. They said, "Better yet, go to the clinic." You know, to rest your mind. You know, be sure. So, that's what I did. I come to Cleveland and I lived on 90th and Euclid, which was right across the street from the hospital.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: I went over to the hospital. I was a walk-in. I didn't even call to make an appointment. And I told the girl what -- what happened to me and I gave her my story. She said, "Well, let me see, who can I" -- she says -- she says, "I'll tell you what's best for that." And naturally, she got someone that did that, spinal and cyst work. And he took me right away knowing that -- you know, she told him I was a veteran, that I had been in Aspinwall. And he took me in and looked at it and he says, "You know what?" He says, "You're lucky that they cut you the way they did." He said, "You're going to be happy and thankful as soon as that heals up completely that they did it that way." He says, "You know, there's a reoccurrence rate on this three or four times." In other words, for each operation there's usually three to follow because they hadn't gone deep enough.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: And they leave so much of it in there and it reoccurs again. So, he says, "You're fortunate." He says, "You're healing from the bottom out." So, he stuffed me with sulfum (ph) powder, which they always -- that's what they were doing in those days. I imagine they do the same thing today. And then, I told him, I says, "Listen, I'm unemployed. I've been out of the service over -- over a year now," and I says, "I ran out of my 52-20." That's what we called that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the 52-20 exactly?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: That's the unemployment they gave us, the Government gave us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: For 52 weeks?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Unemployment checks. Yeah. 52 weeks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: 52 weeks, you got how much?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Twenty dollars a week.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: For 52 weeks?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Right. I ran out on that, had no income, and I -- I told him that. And he says, "You go on and get yourself a job." He says, "Do you have any place in mind?" And I says, "Yeah." I says, "I've got some friends working at TavCo." He says, "Well, there's some tough jobs out there, you have to do a lot of lifting, but be careful of what job they give you. Tell them." And he says, "I'll call the doctor," because they give you an entrance. And he says, "But if they turn you down for physical reasons," he says, "you get back to me." I already got a guy on my side that's going to go to fighting battle with me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: So, I went out there and the doctor -- the personnel accepted me and -- because they were looking for ex-GIs, you know, and they were looking for work. And I went to work and I told the doctor about my back injury. And I says, "Will that hold me up?" He says, "Oh, no." He says, "That won't have anything to do with your lifting and that." He says, "You got to be careful," he says, "how you lift." But I worked there off and on three different times. I quit and went back, quit and went back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Would anything stand out -- anything else stand out as a really vivid memory of your wartime experience, anything other than you've already told me?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: No. I pretty well covered it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, you mentioned the Kasserine Pass. Did we cover that?

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Well, the Kasserine Pass was before I was in the outfit. That's when they lost the Squadron down there, almost the complete squadron, almost all our airplanes. That's when the Germans overran our ground forces and we happened to be up close to the line and they got caught up in it. I used to hear that, you know, from the others that were in it. And in fact, there was -- that's why they had that replacement deal going on. There was a lot of boys in Africa and they'd been overseas all that time. They figured they have to come up with some kind of a replacement system. They were doing that with pilots after so many missions. Why not the enlisted men that were over there? That's how that come about. In a way, I could see that. You know, I understood that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: So, I felt pretty good about it. At least I was going over and someone was coming back in my place. But I never did meet the guy. He was already gone when I got there. Because I was at the placement area in -- in Bari. They kept me down there for about a week. And by the time I went up there, he was already gone. Of course, they probably got word that his replacement was in the country, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: But I think I was one of the first guys to go to the First Fighter Group in that state, you know, man-for-man. After that, there were a lot of them coming in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: Coming in replacing mechanics and whatever, supply men. I -- I was the first Air Operation Specialist. I'll never forget that. And the guy that was still there was a Staff Sergeant that I was working with, his name was Feeney (ph), from California. And he saw me come in and he looked at my stripes and he -- he was hoping to get moved up, you know. And I kind of felt sorry for him too, but that wasn't my doing, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: And that's where the deal come in that they call me in, they were going to rank me down. And I says, "Oh, no. No. No." I says, "You know, if I was not efficient and not able to do the work," I says, "that would be different. Or if I was just a rookie or something like that, I'd be different. But I've -- I've got better than three years in the service." I says, "And you're going to rank me?" I says, "If you're going to do that, you're going to have to go with me to the 15th Air Force. I'm going to fight it." Any time they come up with something like that, I always had an out, an argument.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: But they fixed it up. I told them. I told the Colonel, I says, "If -- if you're intelligent enough, you know how to cover that." He says, "What do you mean?" I said, "I manipulated that in the states on a --" they call that table organization, being allowed so many this and that. I told them, I says, "You got a department that hasn't been filled, just use it." That's all you have to do. As long as your tables of organization heads up, equalizes up, you have nothing to worry about. Even if you went over one for a couple months, what's the difference? Who would know?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: They played that on that. See, I did enough paperwork that they couldn't buffalo me in that. I used to send complete units overseas paper wise. In those days, it wasn't like today, you could do it automatically. We used -- you had to cut your stencils and reread them before you read them through the mimeograph machines, so there were no errors in them. Then, when you would run them through that, you'd have to read them totally and double check for spelling and everything, especially serial numbers. You had to be sure they were correct.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Orlando Ribelli
sp.p: I had two civilians working for me, girls, when I was in the headquarters. I was Special Orders Clerk when I was doing that. And we'd, like I said, when they had a squadron or a group going overseas, boom, they'd bring all the names in on sheets of paper for me and we'd have to put it together and send them over as a group. (End of recording.)
